title: Why We Need to Start Teaching History in Kindergarten
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that the early grades should teach real history, and that two recent initiatives, the Fordham standards review and Educating for American Democracy, still endorse superficial K-2 social studies. She opens with a contrast between a first-grade lesson on American symbols and a story-driven unit on the Boston Tea Party, suggesting children would prefer the second. She catalogs what K-2 standards typically contain: context-free lists of people and holidays, the expanding environments approach, and abstractions like then and now. She points to Norway, where storytelling-based history for ages one to six produced durable learning, and to Willingham's warning against waiting for certainty of understanding. The piece ends by noting that reading and math have crowded out social studies despite evidence that more social studies time correlates with higher reading scores.

Norwegian preschool history taught through stories and museum visits shows young children absorb historical knowledge.

Time spent on social studies correlates with higher reading scores, while more time on comprehension skills does not.
quotes: Option One: A lesson about “American symbols”—the bald eagle, the American flag, the Statue of Liberty—which will focus mostly on the concept of a symbol. You’ll hear that the flag’s 13 stars stand for the 13 colonies, and that it symbolizes independence.

But whatever the justification, it’s clear that the current approach bores children, wastes precious time, and prevents our most vulnerable students from being able to keep up with their more privileged peers at higher grade levels.

On national tests, 85% of eighth-graders score below proficient in U.S. history, as do about 75% in geography and civics. Now there’s also hand-wringing about whether it’s possible to teach these subjects in an even-handed way.

The “expanding environments” approach, which starts with “all about me” and moves on gradually to the family, the neighborhood, and so on, on the baseless assumption that young children are primarily interested in their immediate surroundings.

An important insight that the teachers gained,” the Norwegian study reported, “is that repetition over time, year after year, produces results over time. Even if children do not understand the concepts immediately, early experience can lay the foundations for later learning.

But rather than enabling them to soak up rich content, we give them superficiality and abstractions—on the puzzling theory that they’re too young to understand stories about the past but well equipped to grasp abstract concepts like “symbols” and “chronology.
